problem: The answer says 'the number of dissolved ions stays about the same'. That is wrong: one Ca²⁺ is replaced by two Na⁺, so the particle count doubles (4 meq/L of Ca²⁺ becomes 4 meq/L of Na⁺, i.e. twice as many ions). What stays the same is the number of equivalents, and hence roughly the mass of dissolved solids (Ca, 40 g/mol, becomes 2 Na, 46 g/mol).
fix: answer: One Ca²⁺ is replaced by two Na⁺. The equivalents, and so the mass of dissolved solids, stay about the same (it even rises slightly, 40 mg Ca becomes 46 mg Na). Hardness falls because the divalent ion is gone, but total dissolved solids are not reduced.

problem: The rule 'among ions of the same charge, the smaller hydrated ion is often preferred' holds for cation resins (Ca²⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺ > Li⁺) but reverses for strong-base anion resins, where the smaller hydrated ions (OH⁻, F⁻) are least preferred (SO₄²⁻ > NO₃⁻ > Cl⁻ > OH⁻ > F⁻). A student will over-generalise it.
fix: State that for cation resins the ion with the smaller hydrated radius is held more strongly, while for strong-base anion resins the order runs the other way (Cl⁻ > OH⁻ > F⁻).

problem: 'Operating capacity is the smaller useful value between regenerations' is unclear. It mixes the size of the working capacity with the number of regenerations.
fix: Operating capacity is the part of the total capacity actually used in service between two regenerations. It is lower than the total capacity because not every site is regenerated, and design uses it.

problem: The label 'fresh resin' says regeneration produces fresh resin, which contradicts the exam trap 'thinking regeneration creates new resin'.
fix: Relabel the edge regenerate → rinse as 'restored sites' or 'displace regenerant'.

problem: Feed flow is written C and ionic concentration c; the two symbols differ only by case and are easy to confuse in handwritten work.
fix: Use a clearly distinct symbol, e.g. F for feed flow (L/h), and keep c for concentration (eq/L): n = F × t × c and V = n ÷ Q.
